claim: Alzheimer's disease is behaviorally characterized by cognitive declines such as memory loss.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is behaviorally characterized by cognitive declines such as memory loss (Carlesimo and Oscar-Berman, 1992; Salmon and Bondi, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Carlesimo and Oscar-Berman, 1992 and Salmon and Bondi, 2009

claim: Alzheimer's disease is pathologically defined by β-amyloid plaques and tau pathology including neurofibrillary tangles and tau-mediated neurodegeneration.
source: but pathologically defined by β-amyloid plaques and tau pathology including neurofibrillary tangles and tau-mediated neurodegeneration (Wenk, 2003; Ashe and Zahs, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Wenk, 2003 and Ashe and Zahs, 2010

claim: Memory deficits are necessarily produced by the memory-processing neural circuits in vivo.
source: Because memory deficits are necessarily produced by the memory-processing neural circuits in vivo (Dickerson and Eichenbaum, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Dickerson and Eichenbaum, 2010

claim: Both β-amyloid and tau pathologies are likely involved in memory loss.
source: Both the β-amyloid and tau pathologies are likely involved in the memory loss (Chapman et al., 1999; Yu et al., 2001; Cacucci et al., 2008; Ashe and Zahs, 2010; Palop and Mucke, 2010)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Chapman et al., 1999; Yu et al., 2001; Cacucci et al., 2008; Ashe and Zahs, 2010; Palop and Mucke, 2010

claim: Tau pathology and subsequent neurodegeneration play a key role in mediating the memory symptoms seen at a mature stage of Alzheimer's disease.
source: In particular, tau pathology and subsequent neurodegeneration play a key role in mediating the memory symptoms seen at a mature stage of AD (Ashe and Zahs, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ashe and Zahs, 2010

claim: It is currently unknown how the mnemonic functions of hippocampus are altered by tau pathology in vivo.
source: Currently, it is unknown how the mnemonic functions of HP are altered by tau pathology in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field

claim: Spatial memories in both rodents and humans are encoded by hippocampal place cells that fire at one or a few specific locations of a given space.
source: It is believed that spatial memories in both rodents and humans are encoded by HP place cells that fire at one or a few specific locations of a given space (place fields) (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993; Burgess and O'Keefe, 2003; Ekstrom et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993; Burgess and O'Keefe, 2003; Ekstrom et al., 2003

claim: When an animal runs along a novel spatial trajectory, external sensory input at individual locations drives place cells to fire in a unique sequence, yielding a memory code for the trajectory.
source: When the animal runs along a novel spatial trajectory, external sensory input at individual locations along the trajectory drives place cells to fire one after another in a unique sequence, which yields a memory code for the trajectory (Wilson and McNaughton, 1993; Harris et al., 2003; Dragoi and Buzsaki, 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to Wilson and McNaughton, 1993; Harris et al., 2003; Dragoi and Buzsaki, 2006

claim: After novel experience, the firing sequence becomes internally established and can be reactivated during later memory recall and/or consolidation with or without partial external input.
source: After the novel experience, the sequence becomes internally established and can be reactivated during later memory recall and/or consolidation with or without partial external input (Buzsaki, 1989; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Nadasdy et al., 1999; Lee and Wilson, 2002; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Diba and Buzsaki, 2007; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2008; Davidson et al., 2009; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Buzsaki, 1989; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Nadasdy et al., 1999; Lee and Wilson, 2002; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Diba and Buzsaki, 2007; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2008; Davidson et al., 2009; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011

claim: The interplay between internal and external inputs is important to memory processing in hippocampus and abnormal interaction may lead to memory interference and/or intrusion.
source: It has been proposed that the interplay between internal and external inputs is important to memory processing in HP and abnormal interaction may lead to memory interference and/or intrusion (Nakazawa et al., 2002; McHugh et al., 2007; Colgin et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Nakazawa et al., 2002; McHugh et al., 2007; Colgin et al., 2008

claim: The rTg4510 mouse model was chosen because its well-characterized pathological and behavioral phenotypes mimic many key features of tau pathology in Alzheimer's disease.
source: This model was chosen because its well-characterized pathological and behavioral phenotypes mimic many key features of tau pathology in AD (Ramsden et al., 2005; Santacruz et al., 2005; Berger et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Ramsden et al., 2005; Santacruz et al., 2005; Berger et al., 2007

claim: In rTg4510 mice, overexpression of a mutated version (P301L) of the human tau gene restricted in the forebrain leads to age-dependent spatial memory deficits, tau neurofibrillary tangles, and neuronal loss.
source: In Tau mice, the overexpression of a mutated version (P301L) of the human tau gene restricted in the forebrain leads to age-dependent spatial memory deficits, tau neurofibrillary tangles, and neuronal loss.
evidence: This is a description of the known phenotype of the rTg4510 mouse model based on established knowledge

claim: A total of 497 CA1 neurons were recorded from eight Tau and six wildtype control mice, all at 7–9 months old.
source: We recorded a total of 497 CA1 neurons from eight Tau and six wildtype (WT) control mice, all at 7–9 months old (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected

claim: There was massive neurodegeneration in Tau mice at 7-9 months of age.
source: Confirming previous studies (Ramsden et al., 2005; Santacruz et al., 2005), there was massive neurodegeneration in Tau mice at this age
evidence: Supported by citations to Ramsden et al., 2005; Santacruz et al., 2005 and confirmed by the current study's observations

claim: The thickness of the CA1 pyramidal layer in hippocampus of Tau mice was on average only 48% of that of WT mice.
source: the thickness of the CA1 pyramidal layer in HP of Tau mice was on average only 48% of that of WT mice (Figure 1 and Table 1)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Table 1

claim: The median firing rate of Tau neurons during track running sessions was not significantly different from that of WT neurons (WT 1.21 Hz, Tau 0.90 Hz, p=0.08).
source: The median firing rate of Tau neurons during the track running sessions was not significantly different from that of WT neurons (median and [10% 90%] range rate: WT 1.21 [0.43 3.60] Hz, Tau 0.90 [0.41 2.75] Hz, p=0.08, ranksum-test, same below unless specified otherwise).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: WT neurons fired spikes at stable, specific locations in every lap that the animal traversed a trajectory.
source: As expected, WT neurons fired spikes at stable, specific locations in every lap that the animal traversed a trajectory.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B

claim: Spikes of Tau neurons were not confined to specific locations.
source: In contrast, spikes of Tau neurons were not confined to specific locations (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B

claim: Tau neurons' spikes were still specific to one or a few locations in each individual lap, but the locations changed from lap to lap.
source: Close visual inspections revealed that Tau neurons' spikes were still specific to one or a few locations in each individual lap, but the locations were changed from lap to lap (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B

claim: The median lap SI of WT neurons was only slightly (21%) greater than that of Tau neurons (WT 2.03 bits/spike, Tau 1.68 bits/spike, p=7.7 × 10−11).
source: The median lap SI of WT neurons was only slightly (21%) greater than that of Tau neurons (Figure 2C; WT 2.03 [1.00 3.09] bits/spike, N = 263; Tau 1.68 [0.84 2.34] bits/spike, N = 262; p=7.7 × 10−11)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The median trajectory SI of WT neurons was much greater (180%) than that of Tau neurons (WT 1.29 bits/spike, Tau 0.46 bits/spike, p=5.3 × 10−39).
source: but the median trajectory SI of WT neurons was much greater (180%) than that of Tau neurons (Figure 2D; WT: 1.29 [0.55 2.61] bits/spike; Tau: 0.46 [0.15 1.29] bits/spike; p=5.3 × 10−39)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Tau neurons showed much lower rate-stability than WT neurons (WT 0.66, Tau 0.075, p=1.7 × 10−70).
source: Tau neurons showed much lower rate-stability than WT neurons (Figure 2E; WT: 0.66 [0.30 0.86]; Tau: 0.075 [0.0042 0.34]; p=1.7 × 10−70)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Tau neurons lost their overall location-specificity, mainly due to unstable firing locations.
source: These results reveal that Tau neurons lost their overall location-specificity, mainly due to unstable firing locations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the spatial information and rate-stability data presented

claim: WT neurons fired one after another with a stable, position-locked sequence in every lap of a trajectory.
source: Because WT neurons fired at stable locations, they fired one after another with a stable, position-locked sequence in every lap of a trajectory (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3A

claim: Despite their unstable firing locations, Tau neurons still maintained stable firing sequences, firing with consistent orders across laps.
source: To our surprise, despite their unstable firing locations, Tau neurons still maintained stable firing sequences, that is, they fired with consistent orders across laps (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3A

claim: A total of 13 template sequences were derived from WT mice and 8 from Tau mice.
source: A total of 13 template sequences were derived from WT mice and 8 from Tau mice (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 2

claim: A significant number of detected sequences were found for 9 out of the 13 WT templates and 6 of the 8 Tau templates (p<0.05).
source: We found a significant number of detected sequences for 9 out of the 13 WT templates and 6 of the 8 Tau templates (p<0.05, Z-test; Table 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Table 2

claim: The mean Z-scores for all WT and all Tau templates were similarly high (WT: 2.5 ± 0.3; Tau: 2.3 ± 0.3; p=0.67).
source: The mean (±SEM) Z-scores for all WT and all Tau templates were similarly high (Figure 3B; WT: 2.5 ± 0.3; Tau: 2.3 ± 0.3; p=0.67, one tailed t-test, same below unless specified otherwise).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Both WT and Tau template sequences were detected in almost every lap.
source: Both WT and Tau template sequences were detected in almost every lap (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3A

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of sequences per lap between WT and Tau (WT: 1.0 ± 0.1 times per lap; Tau: 1.4 ± 0.3 times per lap; p=0.10).
source: Although it appeared that Tau sequences occurred more frequently than WT sequences in a given lap (Figure 3A), this difference was not significant (Figure 3C; WT: 1.0 ± 0.1 times per lap; Tau: 1.4 ± 0.3 times per lap; p=0.10).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Tau neurons, like WT neurons, formed robust firing sequences.
source: These results show that Tau neurons, like WT neurons, formed robust firing sequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sequence detection data presented

claim: WT template sequences predominantly occurred at similar locations across laps, whereas Tau sequences shifted their locations from lap to lap.
source: However, there was a major difference between WT and Tau sequences. Whereas WT template sequences predominantly occurred at similar locations across laps, Tau sequences shifted their locations from lap to lap (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3A

claim: The mean location shift of the detected Tau template sequences was significantly greater than that of WT sequences (WT: 12.7 ± 1.9 cm; Tau: 31.3 ± 6.2 cm; p=0.0035).
source: The mean location shift of the detected Tau template sequences was significantly greater than that of WT sequences (Figure 3D; WT: 12.7 ± 1.9 cm; Tau: 31.3 ± 6.2 cm; p=0.0035).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Unlike WT sequences, Tau sequences were not anchored to specific spatial locations.
source: Therefore, unlike WT sequences, Tau sequences were not anchored to specific spatial locations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the location shift data

claim: 74 WT and 68 Tau neurons were active in at least one open box session.
source: We analyzed 74 WT and 68 Tau neurons that were active in at least one open box session.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data analyzed

claim: The median firing rate of Tau neurons in the open box was lower than that of WT neurons (WT 1.3 Hz, Tau 0.9 Hz, p=0.0001).
source: The median firing rate of these Tau neurons was lower than that of WT neurons (WT 1.3 [0.5 3.8] Hz, Tau 0.9 [0.5 2.7] Hz, p=0.0001)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Firing activities of Tau neurons covered a much larger portion of the open box than those of WT neurons.
source: As illustrated by their rate maps (Figure 4B), firing rate color-plotted at each position of the two dimensional (2D) open box, firing activities of Tau neurons covered a much larger portion of the box (meaning less location-specific) than those of WT neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4B

claim: The median open SI of WT neurons was significantly greater than that of Tau neurons (WT: 0.24, Tau: 0.11, p=1.9 × 10−7).
source: The median open SI of WT neurons was significantly greater than that of Tau neurons (Figure 4C; WT: 0.24 [0.04 0.76], N = 131; Tau: 0.11 [0.04 0.34], N = 119; p=1.9 × 10−7).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Tau neurons fired with low location-specificity in the familiar open box.
source: The result indicates that Tau neurons fired with low location-specificity in the familiar open box.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the open SI data

claim: Tau neuron sequences, but not WT sequences, during the track running also appeared frequently during the open box sessions.
source: when we arranged the neurons according to their firing orders in the template sequences derived during track running, it became apparent that Tau neuron sequences, but not WT sequences, during the track running also appeared frequently during the open box sessions (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5A

claim: A significant number of sequences were found in 10 out of the 16 searches in Tau mice, whereas only in 2 of the 24 searches in WT mice (p<0.05).
source: We found a significant number of sequences in 10 out of the 16 searches in Tau mice, whereas only in 2 of the 24 searches in WT mice (p<0.05, Z-test; Table 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Table 2

claim: The mean Z-score of all searches in Tau mice was significantly higher than that in WT mice (WT: −0.1 ± 0.3; Tau: 1.4 ± 0.4; p=0.001).
source: The mean Z-score of all searches in Tau mice was significantly higher than that in WT mice (Figure 5B; WT: −0.1 ± 0.3; Tau: 1.4 ± 0.4; p=0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Tau sequences, but not WT sequences, seen on the track trajectories also appeared robustly during the open box sessions.
source: Therefore, Tau sequences, but not WT sequences, seen on the track trajectories also appeared robustly during the open box sessions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sequence detection data in open box sessions

claim: The paths of detected Tau sequences appeared to be randomly distributed in the open box.
source: To examine this possibility, we plotted the animal's paths between the start and end times of all detected Tau sequences in a search. These paths appeared to be randomly distributed in the box (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5C

claim: The vectors of Tau sequence paths in the open box had no preferred direction (Rayleigh p≥0.07 for all 10 searches).
source: For each search in Tau mice where a significant number of sequences were found, we computed a Rayleigh p value, which tested a null hypothesis that the vectors had no preferred direction. None of the p values for all the 10 searches was significant (Figure 5E, p≥0.07)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: The detected Tau sequences in open box sessions were not due to repetitive running behavior.
source: Therefore, the detected Tau sequences in open box sessions were not due to repetitive running behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Rayleigh test results

claim: Tau sequences seen in the open box were not primarily driven by spatial locations.
source: Together with the low location-specificity of Tau neurons in the open box sessions (Figure 4), we concluded that Tau sequences seen in the open box were not primarily driven by spatial locations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combination of low location-specificity and non-repetitive path data

claim: Tau sequences seen in the open box were the same as those during the track running.
source: Even further, these Tau sequences seen in the open box were the same as those during the track running.
evidence: This is based on the template matching analysis showing the same sequences appeared in both contexts

claim: Tau sequences did not distinguish two completely different spaces during two very different behaviors.
source: Therefore, Tau sequences did not distinguish two completely different spaces during two very different behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that the same sequences appeared on the track and in the open box

claim: This finding is striking given the well-known phenomenon of 'remapping' of place cell activities between different environments.
source: This is a striking result given the well-known phenomenon of 'remapping' of place cell activities between different environments (Muller and Kubie, 1987; Leutgeb et al., 2005; Colgin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison to established knowledge about place cell remapping, supported by citations to Muller and Kubie, 1987; Leutgeb et al., 2005; Colgin et al., 2008

claim: On the novel track, 79 WT neurons and 92 Tau neurons were active on at least one of its trajectories.
source: On the novel track (Figure 6A), 79 WT neurons and 92 tau neurons were active on at least one of its trajectories.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data analyzed

claim: The median firing rates of WT and Tau neurons during the novel track running sessions were not significantly different (WT: 1.4 Hz, Tau: 1.1 Hz, p=0.71).
source: Their median firing rates during the novel track running sessions were not significantly different (WT: 1.4 [0.4 2.7] Hz, Tau: 1.1 [0.4 3.3] Hz, p=0.71).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The firing locations of WT neurons became stabilized quickly on the novel trajectories, whereas those of Tau neurons stayed unstable from lap to lap.
source: Whereas the firing locations of WT neurons became stabilized quickly on the novel trajectories, those of Tau neurons stayed unstable from lap to lap (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6B

claim: The median trajectory SI of Tau neurons on the novel track was much lower than that of WT neurons (WT 0.69 bits/spike, Tau 0.28 bits/spike, p=5.9 × 10−31).
source: As a result, the median trajectory SI of Tau neurons was much lower than that of WT neurons (WT 0.69 [0.23 1.5] bits/spike, Tau 0.28 [0.086 0.68] bits/spike, p=5.9 ×1 0−31)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The median lap SI of WT and Tau neurons on the novel track was similar (WT 1.2 bits/spike, Tau 1.2 bits/spike, p=0.62).
source: despite a similar median lap SI (WT 1.2 [0.58 1.8] bits/spike, Tau 1.2 [0.46 1.6] bits/spike, p=0.62).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The rate-stability of Tau neurons on the novel track was much lower than that of WT neurons (WT 0.47, Tau 0.10, p=1.6 × 10−51).
source: The rate-stability of Tau neurons was much lower than that of WT neurons (WT 0.47 [0.17 0.85], Tau 0.10 [0.03 0.28], p=1.6 × 10−51).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: In the novel open box, 74 WT neurons and 61 Tau neurons were active in at least one session.
source: In the novel open box (Figure 6C), 74 WT neurons and 61 Tau neurons were active in at least one session.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data analyzed

claim: The median firing rates of WT and Tau neurons during the novel box sessions were not significantly different (WT: 1.1 Hz, Tau: 1.0 Hz, p=0.38).
source: The median firing rates of these WT and Tau neurons during the novel box sessions were not significantly different (WT: 1.1 [0.4 2.9] Hz, Tau: 1.0 [0.5 2.6] Hz, p=0.38).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The rate maps of Tau neurons in the novel open box showed much broader firing areas than those of WT neurons.
source: The rate maps of Tau neurons showed much broader firing areas than those of WT neurons (Figure 6D)
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6D

claim: The median open SI of Tau neurons in the novel open box was significantly lower than that of WT neurons (WT: 0.28 Hz, Tau: 0.08 Hz, p=1.3 × 10−12).
source: This was confirmed by the result that the median open SI of Tau neurons was significantly lower than that of WT neurons (WT: 0.28 [0.06 0.71] Hz, Tau: 0.08 [0.02 0.32] Hz, p=1.3 × 10−12).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Tau neurons fired with little location-specificity either on the novel trajectories or in the novel open box.
source: These results show that Tau neurons fired with little location-specificity either on the novel trajectories or in the novel open box.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial information data in novel environments

claim: Tau neurons, like WT neurons, fired with robust sequences on the novel trajectories.
source: Nevertheless, Tau neurons, like WT neurons, fired with robust sequences on the novel trajectories.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6E

claim: Unlike WT neuron sequences, Tau sequences on the novel trajectories were not anchored to specific locations.
source: But unlike WT neuron sequences, Tau sequences on the novel trajectories were not anchored to specific locations (Figure 6E)
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6E

claim: The same Tau sequences seen on novel trajectories also appeared in the novel open box sessions.
source: and same sequences also appeared in the novel open box sessions (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6F

claim: 15 high-order template sequences were derived on the novel trajectories from WT mice and 8 from Tau mice.
source: We derived 15 high-order template sequences on the novel trajectories from WT mice and 8 from Tau mice (Table 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 3

claim: The mean Z-scores of WT and Tau template sequences on the novel trajectories were similarly high (WT: 2.5 ± 0.2, Tau: 2.4 ± 0.4, p=0.91).
source: The mean Z-scores of WT and Tau template sequences on the novel trajectories were similarly high (Figure 6G, WT: 2.5 ± 0.2, Tau: 2.4 ± 0.4, p=0.91)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6G

claim: The mean location shift of Tau sequences on the novel track among laps was greater than that of WT ones (WT: 9.2 ± 0.9 cm, Tau: 18.5 ± 3.6 cm, p=0.0038).
source: but the mean location shift of Tau sequences among laps was greater than that of WT ones (Figure 6H; WT: 9.2 ± 0.9 cm, Tau: 18.5 ± 3.6 cm, p=0.0038).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6H

claim: Tau template sequences were detected in the novel open box sessions significantly more often than WT templates (WT: 0.5 ± 0.2, Tau: 1.5 ± 0.3, p=0.0029).
source: Finally, Tau template sequences were detected in the novel open box sessions significantly more often than WT templates (Figure 6I, mean Z-scores: WT: 0.5 ± 0.2, N = 30 searches; Tau: 1.5 ± 0.3, N = 12; p=0.0029).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6I

claim: The novel open box sessions preceded the novel track running.
source: Here we emphasize that the novel open box sessions preceded the novel track running.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental procedure

claim: Tau sequences seen on the novel trajectories were already preexistent in the prior open box sessions.
source: Therefore, Tau sequences seen on the novel trajectories were already preexistent in the prior open box sessions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that sequences appeared in the open box before the track running

claim: The formation of Tau sequences did not primarily depend on spatial experience in an environment.
source: These findings suggest that the formation of Tau sequences did not primarily depend on spatial experience in an environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that sequences appeared before spatial experience on the track

claim: Randomly sliding rate curves of individual laps significantly reduced the median rate-stability of Tau neurons on both familiar and novel trajectories.
source: Indeed, randomly sliding rate curves of individual laps further significantly reduced the median rate-stability of Tau neurons on both familiar (−0.0020 [−0.034 0.042], p=9.3 × 10−49 compared with actual rate-stability) and novel (−0.0020 [−0.032 0.049], p=1.8 × 10−60) trajectories
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of shuffled data compared to actual data

claim: Spatial locations still modulated Tau neurons' firing activities.
source: indicating that spatial locations still modulated Tau neurons' firing activities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the shuffling analysis showing that actual data differs from random

claim: On the familiar track, the mean Z-scores of Self and ST were similar for both WT (Self 2.5 ± 0.3, ST 2.3 ± 0.2, p=0.53) and Tau (Self 2.3 ± 0.3, ST 1.6 ± 0.5, p=0.27) sequences.
source: On the familiar track, the mean Z-scores of Self and ST were similar for both WT (Self 2.5 ± 0.3, N = 13 templates; ST 2.3 ± 0.2, N = 13; p=0.53) and Tau (Self 2.3 ± 0.3, N = 8; ST 1.6 ± 0.5, N = 8; p=0.27) sequences
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: On the familiar track, there was a significant difference between Self and OT for both WT (OT 0.29 ± 0.3, p=5.8 × 10−6) and Tau (OT 0.10 ± 0.2, p=6.1 × 10−5) sequences.
source: but there was a significant difference between Self and OT for both WT (OT 0.29 ± 0.3, N = 13; p=5.8 × 10−6) and Tau (OT 0.10 ± 0.2, N = 8; p=6.1 × 10−5) sequences (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Tau sequences, like WT sequences, occurred consistently on same trajectories across different sessions and distinguished between different trajectories within same sessions on the familiar track.
source: The result shows that Tau sequences, like WT sequences, occurred consistently on same trajectories across different sessions and distinguished between different trajectories within same sessions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Self/ST/OT comparison on the familiar track

claim: On the novel track, the mean Z-scores of Self and ST remain comparable for both WT (Self 2.5 ± 0.2, ST 1.7 ± 0.3, p=0.06) and Tau (Self 2.4 ± 0.4, ST 2.6 ± 0.6, p=0.79) sequences.
source: On the novel track, whereas the mean Z-scores of Self and ST remain comparable for both WT (Self 2.5 ± 0.2, N = 15; ST 1.7 ± 0.3, N = 15; p=0.06) and Tau (Self 2.4 ± 0.4, N = 8; ST 2.6 ± 0.6, N = 4; p=0.79) sequences
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: On the novel track, there was a significant difference between Self and OT only for WT (OT −0.26 ± 0.2, p=3.0 × 10−9), but not for Tau (OT 1.9 ± 0.5, p=0.51) sequences.
source: there was a significant difference between Self and OT only for WT (OT −0.26 ± 0.2, N = 15; p=3.0 × 10−9), but not for Tau (OT 1.9 ± 0.5, N = 8; p=0.51) sequences (Figure 7B)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: Tau sequences, unlike WT sequences, did not distinguish the two trajectories on the novel track.
source: suggesting that Tau sequences, unlike WT sequences, did not distinguish the two trajectories on the novel track.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Self/OT comparison on the novel track

claim: Tau sequences were originally not trajectory-selective on the novel track, but became so on the familiar track.
source: This analysis shows that Tau sequences were originally not trajectory-selective on the novel track, but became so on the familiar track.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the trajectory selectivity on familiar vs novel tracks

claim: Although Tau neuron's firing activities were not location-specific and Tau sequences were not primarily driven by space, there was still a modulation of Tau neuron's firing activities by spatial experience and spatial trajectory.
source: Therefore, although Tau neuron's firing activities were not location-specific and Tau sequences were not primarily driven by space, there was still a modulation of Tau neuron's firing activities by spatial experience and spatial trajectory.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trajectory selectivity analysis and shuffling analysis

claim: Neighboring WT sequences in track sessions displayed a consistent spatial gap with periodic peaks in their spatial auto-correlograms at the track length.
source: Neighboring WT sequences in track sessions displayed a consistent spatial gap and there were periodic peaks in their spatial auto-correlograms (Figure 8A, left). The spatial period was the same as the track length (∼2 m for the familiar track, ∼1 m for the novel track)
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8A

claim: Tau sequences during track sessions did not show any consistent spatial or temporal gaps and no obvious, periodic peaks were observed in either the spatial or temporal auto-correlograms.
source: In contrast, Tau sequences during track sessions did not show any consistent spatial or temporal gaps in their raster plots and no obvious, periodic peaks were observed in either the spatial or temporal auto-correlograms (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8B

claim: Tau sequences in open box sessions did not show apparent spatial or temporal periodicity.
